title: Nick Meister’s Profile
text:
Current and Future Research
I embody the principle that diverse life experiences enrich scholarly inquiry, demonstrating that non-traditional paths lead to innovative research that addresses complex problems beyond the scope of any single discipline.
This seems to be the direction of my future research:

Disciplines: The application of cognitive science theories and methods to information science and knowledge organization systems (and vice versa). Always with a preference for interdisciplinary research.
Methodology: Developing valid quantitative indicators and computational methods to operationally measure abstract constructs (e.g., translation equivalence, interdisciplinarity, or relevance).
Topics: Usually involving the topics of language, meaning, cognition, and representation. This can manifest in or involve psycholinguistics, cognitive linguistics, natural language processing, translation studies, knowledge representation, semiotics, and information retrieval.

I usually describe my research interests as my “continuously evolving constellation of interests.” A constellation is a decent characterization as, despite being tremendously expansive and diverse, there is structure, and my joy is in the intersection of seemingly unrelated topics, concepts, and disciplines. My diverse academic background has either been the cause or effect of becoming energized when I can connect or apply ideas across disciplines.
Across and within those disciplines, I have come to see that my research interests usually jump back and forth between the extremes of the theoretical-applied continuum. Furthermore, I believe that my most exciting work is when I am bridging those extremes.
The concepts, methods, and disciplines in my constellation of interests as well as their distribution along the theoretical-applied continuum are continuously evolving, but I have found recurring themes. My fundamental interests include meaning, cognition, representation, language, systems, measurement, complexity, emergence, causality, randomness, inference, patterns, connections, ontology, epistemology, information, modeling and construct validity, as well as quantitative and computational methods.

text:
About This Document
This document contains material from my larger cognitive research project. (The LIS 4901 Capstone paper was a very distilled version of that document.) It is a deliberate editorial selection from the full architecture, retaining the experimental design, statistical analysis plan, and theoretical contributions most relevant to a psycholinguistics audience while condensing material whose primary audience is library and information science (I am currently organizing the LIS version). Please note that this document continues to be updated; you can find the version number and last revised date on the title page.
The interdisciplinary nature of my research tends to result in any document drawing simultaneously on several distinct fields of inquiry. No single reader is likely to arrive fluent in all of them; most will be expert in one, two, or three and unfamiliar with the others (I myself am certainly not an expert in most).
Cognitive warrant (in its iteration in this research document) integrates seven distinct knowledge domains. The table below names each area and identifies the specific construct from that area the framework imports.
(I am working on a document to cover the prerequisite terrain for each field and provide a curated, centralized reading to bring a motivated reader to the threshold of genuine engagement with the research document. The goal is not exhaustive coverage of any area but to provide the minimum working fluency required to follow the argument.)







Area
Key Constructs Imported




Library and Information Science (LIS) & Knowledge Organization (KO)
Literary and user warrant; controlled vocabularies; Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) authority record structure; Metadata Authority Description Schema/Resource Description Framework (MADS/RDF); library discovery systems; information (searching) behavior


Lexical Semantics & Psycholinguistics
Polysemes, homonyms, synonyms, and hyponyms; hybrid meaning theory (Trott & Bergen, 2023); primed sensibility judgment task


Distributional Semantics & Natural Language Processing (NLP)
BERT contextual embeddings; cosine distance as continuous semantic proxy; surprisal (context-dependent lexical predictability)


Information Theory (Shannon, 1948)
Entropy; binary entropy function; (conditional) mutual information; conditional independence; Jensen’s inequality


Graph Theory
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG); path distance and lowest common ancestor; implementation in NetworkX


Statistical Modeling
Logistic regression; cross-classified mixed-effects models; likelihood ratio test; natural spline interaction; generalized additive model; Firth’s penalized-likelihood refit


Philosophy of science
(Chang, 2004; Trott & Parkinson-Coombs, 2026): construct validity; the problem of nomic measurement; epistemic iteration

title: Surrogate-Assisted pCI-Gradient Ascent
text:
About This Document
In Section 3.5 of my research document From Literary Warrant to Cognitive Warrant, I stated:

The per-item resolution of \(\mathrm{pCI}\) opens a further application beyond diagnosis. The fitted mixed-effects model that produces \(\mathrm{pCI}\) scores serves a dual function: it is both a diagnostic and a surrogate for predicting the cognitive-information consequences of proposed graph edits to the LCSH DAG, without requiring new behavioral data collection after each proposed change. This surrogate capacity means the model can in principle be extended into a prescriptive optimization procedure rather than a purely descriptive one. The result is a ranked agenda specifying not only which heading assignments are cognitively problematic, but what editorial action—reassignment, record splitting, or BT/NT restructuring—would most improve the aggregate cognitive warrant score.This , and the combinatorial optimization framework it requires, are developed in a companion technical document and are outside the scope of the present study; once run, the behavioral experiments described here will provide the fitted model that makes the procedure executable.

This document starts where pointwise cognitive information left off – a prioritized list of problematic subject headings identified by a negative \(\mathrm{pCI}\) but no specification of what editing actions the cataloger should take. The surrogate-assisted pCI-gradient ascent algorithm fills that gap. Its output is a sequence of recommended edit operations for the cataloger or editor of the KOS, interpretable to an information professional without quantitative training—each recommendation is a specific, named edit to a specific, named authority record.
Together, pCI and the algorithm constitute a complete empirical reform pipeline for knowledge organization systems. It is important to note, however, that it does not supplant literary warrant, cultural warrant, and professional expertise as necessary inputs to any final editorial decision. What the procedure adds is a quantitative, behaviorally grounded “first filter” that directs expert attention toward the changes most likely to improve the cognitive accessibility of the vocabulary for its users.

title: Research Hub for Cognitive Warrant and the Empirical Evaluation of LCSH
text:
This site organizes materials related to my LIS 4901 capstone project, Cognitive Warrant: A Theoretical Framework for Evaluating Semantic Alignment in Knowledge Organization Systems, as part of my requirements for the Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) degree at the University of Denver.
The project investigates whether the categorical and hierarchical structures of the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) correspond to measurable patterns in our semantic cognition. Substituting LCSH boundaries for dictionary-derived sense boundaries, the study replicates the primed sensibility judgment paradigm of Trott and Bergen (2023) and extends their hybrid meaning theory through a novel heading appropriateness rating paradigm.

Knowledge organization systems do not merely describe the world – they impose structure on how users encounter it.
The purpose of this study is to develop and empirically evaluate the concept of cognitive warrant as a principle for knowledge organization, defined as the extent to which the categorical and structural distinctions encoded in a knowledge organization system correspond to observable patterns in human semantic processing.
Cognitive warrant, therefore, becomes a falsifiable claim: that professionally imposed boundaries track psychologically meaningful partitions in semantic space.
Cognitive warrant positions knowledge organization research to engage empirically with the semantic processing and cognitive structure of the users library discovery systems are designed to serve.

title: Cognitive Warrant Analytic Pipeline
text:
This page is a narrated version of the analysis pipeline described in Chapter 5 of my research document (“The Analytic Pipeline: Logistic Regression and the Estimation of Cognitive Warrant Metrics”). It runs the pipeline on the real merged Experiment 2 / LCSH dataset and is published here, in the style of Trott and Bergen’s own pre-registration code, so that other researchers can inspect, reproduce, and critique every step – including the diagnostic dead ends and corrections that shaped the final approach.
The pipeline takes each stimulus pair (a prime sentence and a target sentence sharing a word, drawn from Trott and Bergen’s Experiment 2) and asks how much information a predictor – BERT cosine distance (\(d\)), LCSH heading congruence (\(S\)), or LCSH hierarchical distance (\(h\)) – carries about whether the pair reflects the same underlying sense (\(Y\)). That question is operationalized as cognitive information, \(CI(d)\): the reduction in the entropy of \(Y\) once the predictor is known, expressed in bits.
At a high level, the pipeline:

Restructures trial-level records (repeated measures) into one row per unique stimulus pair.
Runs diagnostics that determine how the rest of the pipeline should be interpreted – most importantly, whether the LCSH-derived predictor \(S\) is empirically informative or a tautological restatement of the outcome.
Fits baseline (Y ~ d) and full (Y ~ d + S) logistic models, using Firth’s bias-reduced estimator where ordinary glm() shows separation.
Converts fitted probabilities to entropy, then to piecewise and pointwise cognitive information.
Repeats the same pipeline with hier_distance (recoded as h_finite) in place of S, since S turns out to be tautologically identical to the outcome in this dataset (see Data diagnostics).
Saves all tables, plots, and fitted models used elsewhere in the write-up.

Required packages: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "logistf", "lme4", "splines", "patchwork", "knitr")).


Code
library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and plotting
library(logistf)   # Firth's bias-reduced logistic regression (stable under separation)
library(lme4)      # generalized linear mixed-effects models (random-intercept robustness check)
library(splines)   # loaded for parity with the modeling scripts that build on this one
library(patchwork) # combines separate ggplots into one figure
library(knitr)      # renders the LaTeX table at the end of this page

section: Step 0: Load and restructure trial-level records
text:
Step 0: Load and restructure trial-level records
The trial-level file inherits the repeated-measures structure of Trott and Bergen’s Experiment 2: 187 subjects, each responding to a subset of stimulus pairs. This step collapses that structure down to one row per unique (word, version_with_order) pair, which is the unit of analysis for everything that follows.
This walkthrough reads tb2023_exp2_lcsh_distances.csv from assets/data/, the copy of the merged dataset committed to the public repository (the working copy under data/processed/, produced by get_distances.py, is regenerated locally and excluded from version control). Paths below are relative to this file’s location in pages/, so the page renders correctly both locally and as part of the built site.


Code
raw <- read_csv("../assets/data/tb2023_exp2_lcsh_distances.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# distance_elmo_lcsh is entirely missing in this file (the LCSH-anchored ELMo
# frame was never computed) -- dropped rather than carried as an all-NA column.
raw <- raw %>% select(-distance_elmo_lcsh)


same, same_heading, hier_distance, distance_bert, ambiguity_type, and Class are all properties of the stimulus pair, not of the trial – each should take exactly one value within every (word, version_with_order) group. The check below confirms that empirically rather than assuming it; if it ever fails on a future data pull, that is a signal to stop and investigate before trusting the collapse that follows.


Code
pair_key <- c("word", "version_with_order")
pair_level_cols <- c("same", "same_heading", "hier_distance", "same_nbhd",
                      "distance_bert", "distance_bert_lcsh", "distance_elmo",
                      "ambiguity_type", "Class")

nun_check <- raw %>%
  group_by(across(all_of(pair_key))) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(pair_level_cols), n_distinct), .groups = "drop")

stopifnot(all(nun_check[pair_level_cols] == 1))
message("Pair-level covariates confirmed constant within (word, version_with_order).")


Pair-level covariates confirmed constant within (word, version_with_order).


With that confirmed, each pair is reduced to a single row. A trial-level summary (mean accuracy, mean log RT, subject/trial counts) is kept alongside it in case RT or accuracy covariates are wanted for a robustness check later – it is not used by the \(CI(d)\) pipeline itself, which operates on \(Y_i\) = same, not on RT or accuracy.


Code
trial_summary <- raw %>%
  group_by(across(all_of(pair_key))) %>%
  summarise(
    n_trials     = n(),
    n_subjects   = n_distinct(subject),
    mean_correct = mean(correct_response),
    mean_log_rt  = mean(log_rt),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

pairs_df <- raw %>%
  distinct(across(all_of(c(pair_key, pair_level_cols)))) %>%
  left_join(trial_summary, by = pair_key) %>%
  mutate(
    pair_id = paste(word, version_with_order, sep = "__"),
    Y       = as.integer(same),          # Y_i: ground-truth same-sense indicator
    S       = as.integer(same_heading),  # S_i: LCSH heading congruence
    d       = distance_bert,             # d_i: BERT cosine distance (unmodified frame)
    h       = hier_distance              # h_i: BT/NT shortest-path distance
                                          #      (Inf if S_i = 0 with no shared ancestor
                                          #      within the search horizon)
  )

message(sprintf(
  "Collapsed %d trial-level rows (%d subjects) into %d unique stimulus pairs across %d words.",
  nrow(raw), n_distinct(raw$subject), nrow(pairs_df), n_distinct(pairs_df$word)
))


Collapsed 2403 trial-level rows (187 subjects) into 299 unique stimulus pairs across 25 words.

title: Cognitive Warrant Analytic Pipeline
text:
Data diagnostics
These checks run before any downstream number is trusted, because they determine how the rest of the pipeline should be read.

Is \(S\) perfectly collinear with \(Y\)?
This is the single most consequential check in the pipeline. If same_heading (\(S\)) is identical to same (\(Y\)) for every pair, the “full model” logistic regression of \(Y\) on \(d\) and \(S\) is not testing whether LCSH heading congruence adds information beyond BERT distance – it is recovering a tautology, because \(S\) was constructed to equal \(Y\) for every pair in this file (each dictionary sense M1/M2 was mapped one-to-one onto a single LCSH authority record). Under that condition, \(CI(d)\) comes out equal to \(H(Y \mid d)\) exactly (up to numerical floor), and warrant efficiency \(\bar\eta\) is \(\approx 1\) everywhere – a mechanical consequence of how same_heading was derived here, not an empirical finding about LCSH’s cognitive value.


Code
same_vs_heading <- mean(pairs_df$Y == pairs_df$S)
message(sprintf("Proportion of pairs where Y (same) == S (same_heading): %.4f", same_vs_heading))


Proportion of pairs where Y (same) == S (same_heading): 1.0000


Code
if (isTRUE(all.equal(same_vs_heading, 1))) {
  warning(paste(
    "same_heading is IDENTICAL to same for every pair in this file.",
    "The baseline-vs-full model comparison below will show a trivial,",
    "perfectly-separated effect of S -- this reflects how the LCSH mapping",
    "was constructed (one heading per dictionary sense), not an empirical",
    "test of whether LCSH boundaries carry information beyond distance.",
    "hier_distance (h), which DOES vary independently of Y among",
    "cross-heading pairs, is the more informative structural variable for",
    "this proof of concept -- see 'Structural extension' below."
  ))
}

baseline-vs-full model comparison below will show a trivial,
perfectly-separated effect of S -- this reflects how the LCSH mapping was
constructed (one heading per dictionary sense), not an empirical test of
whether LCSH boundaries carry information beyond distance. hier_distance (h),
which DOES vary independently of Y among cross-heading pairs, is the more
informative structural variable for this proof of concept -- see 'Structural

Confirmed: same_heading and same agree on every pair in this file. Everything reported under “S (same_heading)” below should be read as a methods validation (does the pipeline recover the expected ceiling case correctly?), not as an empirical test of LCSH’s cognitive value. The empirical test is the hier_distance extension further down.


Where does hier_distance carry information?
hier_distance is Inf for cross-heading pairs with no shared ancestor within the search horizon, and exactly 0 for same-heading pairs (trivially, since a node has zero path length to itself). section: Step 1: Fit baseline and full logistic models
text:
Step 1: Fit baseline and full logistic models
The baseline model estimates \(P(Y=1 \mid d)\); the full model adds \(S\):
\[\text{logit } P(Y=1\mid d) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 d \qquad\qquad \text{logit } P(Y=1\mid d, S) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 d + \gamma_2 S\]
Given the diagnostic above, the full model is expected to show quasi/perfect separation on \(S\): glm() will warn that fitted probabilities are numerically 0 or 1, and the standard error on \(\gamma_2\) will be enormous. The point estimates and fitted probabilities are still usable for the entropy calculations that follow, but the reported p-values and confidence intervals for \(\gamma_2\) are not trustworthy from glm() alone in this degenerate case.


Code
m_baseline <- glm(Y ~ d, data = pairs_df, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
m_full_glm <- glm(Y ~ d + S, data = pairs_df, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

title: Cognitive Warrant Analytic Pipeline
section: Step 2: From fitted probabilities to conditional entropy
text:
Step 2: From fitted probabilities to conditional entropy
The binary entropy function \(H(p) = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p)\) converts a fitted probability into bits of uncertainty about \(Y\).


Code
h_b <- function(p) {
  p <- pmin(pmax(p, 1e-12), 1 - 1e-12)  # guard against log(0)
  -p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)
}

pairs_df <- pairs_df %>%
  mutate(
    H_baseline = h_b(p_baseline),
    H_full     = h_b(p_full)
  )

title: Cognitive Warrant Analytic Pipeline
text:
Step 3: Piecewise (binned) cognitive information, \(CI(d)\)
Pairs are grouped into K = 6 bins of BERT cosine distance – fewer than in the schematic Chapter 5 template, given only 299 pairs in this dataset; re-run with K = 8 or K = 10 as a sensitivity check if extending this analysis.


Code
K <- 6
pairs_df <- pairs_df %>%
  mutate(distance_bin = cut(d, breaks = K, include.lowest = TRUE))


Within each bin, CI_k is computed two ways. H_bar_d (and the resulting CI_k) comes from m_baseline, a model fit independently of m_full_firth, so this version is not guaranteed non-negative by Jensen’s inequality – that guarantee only holds when \(H(Y\mid d)\) is the entropy of the same model’s own \(S\)-marginalized mixture probability, not an independently-estimated stand-in. Within a bin, every pair has an actual observed \(S\), so mean(p_full) (p_bar_full) is already the bin’s true, empirical \(S\)-marginalized probability – no local-window weighting is needed at this level of aggregation. CI_k_v2, built from p_bar_full, is the internally consistent version and is what the rest of this page uses; CI_k is retained alongside for comparison. p_bar_full is also exposed as its own column so Step 4 can reuse it as pCI’s marginal reference.


Code
ci_piecewise <- pairs_df %>%
  group_by(distance_bin) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pairs     = n(),
    x_mid       = mean(d),
    H_bar_d     = mean(H_baseline),
    H_bar_dS    = mean(H_full),
    CI_k        = H_bar_d - H_bar_dS,
    p_bar_full  = mean(p_full),
    H_bar_d_mix = h_b(p_bar_full),
    CI_k_v2     = H_bar_d_mix - H_bar_dS,
    P_d         = n_pairs / nrow(pairs_df),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

A smooth, model-implied \(CI(d)\) curve on a fine grid can be plotted against the piecewise estimate above, and against the theoretical inverted-U prediction (Chapter 4, H3-as-theorem). Because \(S\) is (quasi-)deterministic given \(d\) in this dataset, the population-averaged \(H(Y \mid d, S)\) on the grid is computed by weighting the \(S=0\) and \(S=1\) curves by the empirical \(P(S=1 \mid d)\) at each \(d\), rather than assuming a fixed \(S\). A local (±0.05) empirical window is used as a simple approximation of that weight, falling back to the global mean when no pairs fall in the window.


Code

  mutate(

    p_full_grid_S0  = plogis(predict(m_full_firth, newdata = mutate(grid_d, S = 0), type = "link")),
    p_full_grid_S1  = plogis(predict(m_full_firth, newdata = mutate(grid_d, S = 1), type = "link")),
    H_baseline_grid = h_b(p_baseline_grid)
  )

grid_d <- grid_d %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    pi_S1 = mean(pairs_df$S[abs(pairs_df$d - d) <= 0.05]),

    H_full_grid = pi_S1 * h_b(p_full_grid_S1) + (1 - pi_S1) * h_b(p_full_grid_S0),
    CI_grid = H_baseline_grid - H_full_grid
  ) %>%
  ungroup()


Just as for the piecewise estimate, CI_grid uses H_baseline_grid from m_baseline – a model fit independently of m_full_firth – so it is not guaranteed non-negative. CI_grid_v2 fixes this the same way CI_k_v2 did: by computing \(H(Y\mid d)\) from the full model’s own \(S\)-marginalized mixture probability (p_mix_S) instead. This correction eliminates 85/85 negative grid points at \(d > 0.4\) that appear in the uncorrected version, and is the version used from here on.

grid_d <- grid_d %>%
  mutate(
    p_mix_S  = pi_S1 * p_full_grid_S1 + (1 - pi_S1) * p_full_grid_S0,
    H_true_S = h_b(p_mix_S),
    CI_grid_v2 = H_true_S - H_full_grid
  )

Everywhere else in this stretch, the \(\pm0.05\) window contains only different-heading pairs, so pi_S1 = 0 and CI_grid_v2 collapses to exactly 0 – visible directly above, and in the flat-zero stretches of the plotted curve between bumps.
Why does a brief, small rise in pi_S1 produce such a large bump in \(CI(d)\)? By this point in the pipeline, p_full_grid_S1 (\(\approx 0.95\)-\(0.98\)) and p_full_grid_S0 (\(\approx 0.0005\)-\(0.0015\)) sit at opposite extremes – the conditional model is confident either way, consistent with \(S \approx Y\) almost everywhere (per the diagnostic at the top of this page). But H_true_S is the entropy of the mixture probability, pi_S1\(\cdot p(S{=}1) + (1-\)pi_S1\()\cdot p(S{=}0)\). Since those two probabilities are so far apart, even a small nonzero pi_S1 drags the mixed probability up toward the maximally uncertain 0.5 region – and entropy is sharply concave there, so it swells fast. At \(d \approx 0.54\), for instance, pi_S1 \(\approx 0.4\) pulls the mixed probability to \(\approx 0.38\), which alone is enough to produce the single highest point on the whole curve.
So each peak marks a moment where the sliding window happens to graze one of these four isolated same-heading pairs in an otherwise same-heading-empty region – a fixed-bandwidth local window becoming unstable wherever its conditioning variable is sparse, amplified here by how nonlinear entropy is near \(p=0.5\). Read the piecewise (binned) estimate, ci_piecewise, as the more trustworthy summary of this region: it uses every pair’s own observed \(S\) rather than a local approximation, and does not exhibit this artifact.

title: Cognitive Warrant Analytic Pipeline
text:
Step 4: Pointwise cognitive information, \(pCI_i\)
pCI measures how much a single pair’s outcome is (dis)confirmed by the full model relative to a marginal reference, in bits:
\[pCI_i \equiv \log_2\frac{P(Y_i \mid d_i,\, S_i)}{P(Y_i \mid d_i)} = \log_2\frac{P_{\text{full}}(Y_i)}{P_{\text{marginal}}(Y_i)}\]
The identity “\(E[pCI_i \mid \text{bin } k] = CI_k\) by construction” is a claim about an in-expectation relationship between two log-probability terms computed from the same pair of reference models – it only holds if pCI and CI_k are built from consistent models. Using p_baseline (from m_baseline, fit independently of m_full_firth) as the marginal reference, as in pCI below, introduces a residual term equal to the KL divergence between the true (mixture) distribution and m_baseline’s fitted distribution within each pair’s bin – not sampling noise, but a genuine, bin-varying bias that grows wherever m_baseline is a poor local approximation (the sparse, high-distance bins where this shows up most). pCI_v2, using p_bar_full (the full model’s own bin-mean, \(S\)-marginalized probability, from ci_piecewise) as the marginal reference instead, is the internally consistent version paired with CI_k_v2.


Code
pairs_df <- pairs_df %>%
  mutate(
    p_full_obs     = ifelse(Y == 1, p_full,     1 - p_full),
    p_baseline_obs = ifelse(Y == 1, p_baseline, 1 - p_baseline),
    pCI            = log2(p_full_obs / p_baseline_obs)
  ) %>%
  left_join(ci_piecewise %>% select(distance_bin, p_bar_full), by = "distance_bin") %>%
  mutate(
    p_marginal_obs = ifelse(Y == 1, p_bar_full, 1 - p_bar_full),
    pCI_v2         = log2(p_full_obs / p_marginal_obs)
  )


As an internal consistency check, the mean of pCI_v2 within a bin should approximate that bin’s piecewise CI_k_v2 – the two are computed from different formulas at different levels of aggregation, so agreement indicates the implementation, not just the theory, is behaving as specified.

  group_by(distance_bin) %>%
  summarise(mean_pCI_v2 = mean(pCI_v2), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(ci_piecewise, by = "distance_bin") %>%
  mutate(diff = mean_pCI_v2 - CI_k_v2)

Structural extension: hier_distance as the non-tautological predictor
Because \(S = Y\) exactly in this file, the \(S\)-based \(CI(d)\) above is a ceiling artifact of the mapping, not an empirical result – see Data diagnostics. hier_distance (\(h\)) is not tautologically fixed by \(Y\): among cross-heading pairs (\(S = 0\)), \(h\) takes finite values for pairs sharing a broader term and Inf otherwise, and this variation is independent of the same/different-sense label by construction. A model of \(Y\) using \(d\) and a finite/infinite recoding of \(h\) – rather than \(S\) – is the more informative proof-of-concept computation on this particular file, since its success is not guaranteed by the way the variables were built.

pairs_df <- pairs_df %>%
  mutate(
    h_finite = is.finite(h),                    # TRUE if a shared BT/NT ancestor exists within the search horizon
    h_capped = ifelse(is.finite(h), h, NA_real_) # finite hierarchical distances only
  )

m_full_hier <- glm(Y ~ d + h_finite, data = pairs_df, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

text:
Saving output
Two different things are saved here: (a) the analysis-ready tables and fitted model objects, so downstream work (plots, the write-up, re-checking a number later) doesn’t require re-running the whole pipeline – re-fitting m_full_firth via logistf() is the slow step – and (b) LaTeX-ready table code for dropping directly into the manuscript.
Output is written to cognitive-warrant-pipeline_output/, a directory alongside this page (not tracked in the repository – see .gitignore), so re-rendering never clobbers a previous run’s pipeline_output/ under data/processed/.


Code
out_dir <- "cognitive-warrant-pipeline_output"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# --- Plots, as PNG ---
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "p_ci_overlay.png"), plot = p_ci_overlay,
       width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300)
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "p_ci_hier.png"), plot = p_ci_hier,
       width = 7, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 300)

# --- Tables, as CSV (for re-use, e.g. in a separate plotting script) ---
write_csv(pairs_df,               file.path(out_dir, "pairs_df_full.csv"))

This was the main assignment in my cognitive neuroscience graduate seminar – a grant proposal for a hypothetical research project. This is where I first came across Trott and Bergen (2023), and the proposal is a (novice) attempt at validating their hybrid meaning theory with magnetoencephalography (MEG). I didn’t even know MEG existed before the seminar, but I learned so much about the primary methods and key experimental findings associated with cognitive neuroscience. Needless to say, this was offered by the DU Psychology Department, not the MLIS program. I was very fortunate to get approval to count it as an elective towards my degree. Cognitive warrant and its engagement with LCSH is a direct result of this seminar.

📄 Presentation slides


📄 Poster: LCSH hierarchical subgraph structure
This shows real examples from Trott and Bergen’s stimuli mapped to LCSH. It is the result of a computational pipeline from raw source data to usable graph. The Library of Congress MADS/RDF bulk download — about 330,000 records — was parsed in Python and represented using NetworkX. Each broader term relationship of a subject authority record becomes a directed edge. The result is a directed acyclic graph that supports all the Lowest Common Ancestor algorithms needed for hierarchical distance computation.


📄 Poster: The intellectual landscape of cognitive warrant
Presents the intellectual landscape my research draws from. Each cluster represents a field: knowledge organization, computational semantics, formal foundations (graph theory, information theory, and statistics), psycholinguistics, cognitive science, and research methodology. The central node is cognitive warrant itself. What makes this research distinctive is not just that it touches these fields — it’s that the argument requires all of them simultaneously. No single field contains the tools to answer the question.
